title: The Mighty Angel and the Little Scroll
summary: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a small open scroll. Seven thunders speak, but John is told not to write down what they said. The angel swears that there will be no more delay, and John is told to eat the scroll, which is sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, and is recommissioned to prophesy about many peoples and nations.
story: Chapter 9 ended with a bleak verdict: after the first two woes, humanity did not repent. Before the seventh trumpet sounds (11:15), the book pauses, as it did between the sixth and seventh seals in chapter 7. This interlude turns from judgment to witness. John is given a message to eat and to speak, and chapter 11 will show the church's prophetic witness in the figures of the two witnesses. The angel's oath announces that God's purposes are about to be completed, the very thing the martyrs asked for in 6:10, but the way there runs through the bittersweet calling of prophecy.
historical:
The scene still unfolds in John's vision on Patmos, but the question at its center, how long until God acts, was pressing for first-century believers. 2 Peter 3:4-9 answers scoffers who asked where the promise of Christ's coming was, and Jewish writers of the same period wrestled with God's delay after the destruction of the temple in AD 70. The angel's oath speaks into that longing: the delay is not indifference, and the end is fixed.

The instruction to prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings also placed John, a prisoner on a small island, in the line of Israel's prophets who spoke to empires. Jeremiah was appointed over nations and kingdoms (Jeremiah 1:10), and Daniel spoke to the kings of Babylon and Persia. Whether the chapter looks ahead to events in the first century, in the course of church history, or at the very end depends on the interpretive school; all agree it is a commissioning scene.
cultural:
The chapter leans heavily on Daniel and Ezekiel. In Daniel 12:7 a man clothed in linen, standing above the waters of the river, lifts both hands to heaven and swears by him who lives forever that the end will come after a time, times, and half a time. Here the angel lifts his right hand and swears that there will be no more delay. Daniel was told to seal up the vision until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9); John is told to seal up the thunders, but at the book's close he is told not to seal his prophecy, because the time is near (22:10). Ezekiel was handed a scroll and told to eat it, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 2:8 to 3:3), though he then went out in bitterness of spirit (Ezekiel 3:14). Jeremiah too said God's words were found and he ate them (Jeremiah 15:16).

Thunder is the voice of God in the Old Testament. Psalm 29 describes the voice of the LORD thundering over the waters seven times. Raising the hand was the common gesture of an oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40), and swearing by the creator of heaven, earth, and sea calls the whole created order to witness.
literary: The angel is described in terms close to the risen Christ of chapter 1 (a face like the sun, legs like fire) and the throne of chapter 4 (a rainbow), so he carries heaven's authority, though he is called an angel and swears by God rather than being sworn by. His stance on sea and land claims the whole world. The chapter has three movements: the angel and the forbidden thunders (vv. 1-4), the oath (vv. 5-7), and the eating of the scroll (vv. 8-11). The word mystery in verse 7 points back to the prophets and ahead to the seventh trumpet. The small scroll is described with a diminutive, and whether it is the same scroll the Lamb opened in chapter 5, now handed to the prophet, or a separate message, is debated; the repeated description of it as open suggests its contents are now available for John to proclaim.

outline.t: The mighty angel and the sealed-up thunders
John eats the little scroll and is sent to prophesy again

doctrines.note: God reveals his purposes through the prophets, yet he also withholds: the thunders are sealed. Scripture gives what God's people need to be faithful, not everything they might wish to know (compare Deuteronomy 29:29).
John is sent to prophesy to many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings. The witness of God's people to the world is the next movement of the story, and chapter 11 will develop it.

The angel swears by the one who created heaven, earth, and sea that God's mystery will be fulfilled. History's timetable belongs to its maker, and the delay his people feel is not the absence of a plan.

words.note: Biblaridion, a little scroll, a diminutive of the word used for the sealed scroll in chapter 5. Some read the small size as marking a different, more limited message; others think the diminutive is simply stylistic and the scroll is the one the Lamb opened, now given to the prophet.

Chronos, time. The angel says there will be no more chronos, which the King James Version rendered as time no longer. The sense in context is almost certainly no more delay, answering the martyrs who were told to wait a little longer (6:11, where the same word appears).

Mustērion, mystery. In the New Testament a mystery is not a puzzle but a purpose of God once hidden and now revealed. Paul uses it of the gospel and of the inclusion of the nations (Ephesians 3:3-6). Here the mystery of God is his whole plan for the world, soon to be completed.

Prophēteuō, to prophesy, to speak God's message. In the Bible it includes foretelling but is chiefly forthtelling, declaring God's word to people. John's calling, like Ezekiel's, is to speak a message that is sweet because it is God's and bitter because of what it announces.

christ: Christ is not directly named here, though the angel's appearance recalls the vision of the risen Christ in chapter 1, and a few interpreters identify the angel with him. The chapter's connection to Christ lies in its message and its messenger. The mystery of God announced here is, in the New Testament, the purpose God has revealed in Christ (Colossians 1:26-27), and the kingdom it points to will be declared at the seventh trumpet as the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (11:15). The bittersweet scroll mirrors the shape of the gospel itself: good news that centers on a cross. Those who carry it share the calling of Jesus, the faithful witness (1:5).

hard.q: What did the seven thunders say, and why is John told not to write it down?
hard.a:
Revelation does not tell us, and that silence is itself part of the message. Interpreters offer several explanations. Some think the thunders announced a further series of judgments like the seals and trumpets, and that God cancels it: judgments alone have not produced repentance (9:20-21), so the book turns instead to the witness of the church. Others see a reminder that even an apocalypse, a revealing, does not reveal everything; Paul too heard things he was not permitted to tell (2 Corinthians 12:4). Still others connect it with Daniel's sealed book and suggest the thunders' content belongs to a time not yet come.

What can be said with confidence is that readers should resist building schemes on what God chose not to disclose. The chapter's weight falls on what John is told to do: take the open scroll, take it in, and speak.

questions: John was told not to write down what the thunders said. How do you live with the things God has not explained?
God's word is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach. When has a true word from Scripture been both for you?
The angel declares there will be no more delay. Where are you waiting on God, and how does this chapter speak to that waiting?
